I have to give it credit: Philly didn’t beat around the bush. It made sure I was well aware, within a few weeks of my arrival, that I was not wanted there. That I was an invasive species. That it would punk me until I left.

The stress caused lots of brand-new health problems, which I wasn’t able to address because it was so hard to find local health care. In my three years in the city, I had three gynecologists because the first two disappeared. I was advised to schedule a necessary screening — for an ailment that later landed me in an NYC hospital for emergency surgery* — and was told to “call back next July,” a whole year later. I found a general practitioner I liked, but she could never dedicate more than five minutes to our appointments — and a month before my departure, as she was helping to connect me to surgeons to address another new complication, I learned that she, too, had “left the practice.”

* Before Philly, I had never spent a single night in the hospital!

Philly’s hard water and other unspecified environmental factors did crazy things to my skin and hair, and something caused a perpetual allergic reaction around my eyes, which, according to my long-term NYC optometrist (to whom I’ve recently returned), actually inflamed my eyelids to the point that they temporarily warped my corneas. So that’s why I’ve been unable to focus for the past couple years!

Meanwhile, Andy, who hardly ever got sick in years prior, suffered regular respiratory ailments in Philly.** He rarely had the time or lung capacity to take his bike out for long rides, which has been one of his great joys for decades.

** Update, January 2026: it was cancer — an 8-inch-by-8-inch tumor his inattentive doctors didn’t happen to notice.

In short, the city made its point: we had to go.

I was recruited for a very long time for a very fancy job, yet, when I arrived, pretty much everything that could’ve possibly gone wrong, did. I’ve recounted much of this saga already. I have so many more juicy anecdotes I could share, but I won’t. I need to move on.

Yet I hope you’ll grant me this one last tale: a coda that’s emblematic of the whole tragicomic experience. I resigned in late June. I immediately initiated efforts to re-home hundreds of books and journals: duplicate copies of books I’d been asked to review, comp copies of books I’d purchased separately, full print runs of journals I’d whittled down to pdfs of the most salient articles. At my previous institution, I’d set these extra texts on a table outside my department office — or advertise sizable stocks on the department listserv and invite folks over to our apartment to claim what they wanted. All hand-offs had some degree of humanity.

Here, there was no such infrastructure for organic exchange. After initially sharing an office with emeritus faculty and their furniture and files, I was then moved — for my final two years — to a space in a mostly vacant but charmingly leaky hallway, adjacent to a couple departments with which I had no affiliation. This “temporary” space was about a quarter-mile — through plazas of various elevations, up and down several sets of stairs — from my own department. For a week before my campus security access was terminated, I made multiple daily, sweaty half-hour round trips between the two buildings, lugging books in tote bags for deposit on a communal table amidst various humanities departments, hoping those volumes would all find their readers. By the end of each daily circuit, nearly every book had been claimed, which brought great satisfaction. Still, I was mildly disappointed to realize that their new guardians had no idea of the books’ provenance — nor did they have any idea that I existed.My campus key card was deactivated on July 1 (see, institutions can be efficient in some matters!), so I had to get special permission to access my office for the final move-out. The building was ringed with construction, and there was no nearby parking, so we were told to park in a nearby garage, given roughly an hour to pack everything up and move it to the elevators, then permitted to back our car onto a pedestrian walkway for a speedy load-in. The building manager, like so many campus support staff, was spectacularly kind, conscientious, and helpful.

Our car simply couldn’t accommodate all the remaining material, so I recycled a couple dozen three-ring binders full of lesson plans from my first classes in the early aughts — or I used their pages as packing material. I also hoped to redistribute about 20 remaining books, all in pristine condition, and print runs of several fantastic journals: Critical Inquiry, October, Log, Logic, and more. Time was ticking, so I placed these materials on a communal table in the elevator lobby — a table that housed other orphaned media — hoping passers-through would encounter them and take them home. After I confirmed that the office was empty, and I returned to the lobby for my final descent, I saw someone from a nearby department combing through the piles. That person asked if these materials were mine, noted that they weren’t relevant to their department’s interests, determined that I therefore “can’t use the table,” and informed me that we’d need to move everything to the floor beside the trash cans.

The resources that fed and evidenced twenty three years of pretty damn good work — work somehow, not long before, worthy of enthusiastic recruitment to a presidential professorship — now waited for the landfill. I had to laugh. “Thank you,” I told the stranger, “for the perfect goodbye.”

Philly’s a fine city. My employer simply ruined it for me. I came to dread crossing the Schuylkill River from our home in Center City. Even if I were heading past campus to somewhere delightful, like a friend’s house or Making Worlds Books, the thought of passing through that Zone of Despair manifested a lump in my throat and a weight on my chest. Even the westward journey to visit my family in Central PA elicited dread because it meant braving the always-terrible Schuylkill — aka “Sure Kill” — Expressway, whose inevitable delays made the trip to my childhood home even longer than it had been from NYC.

The only westward trek I relished was the nighttime walk across the river to the train station, one of the few remaining grand urban train depots, which once featured the last split-flat display on the Northeast Corridor — a distinction about which I’ve written. From 30th Street, I commenced my weekly journeys back “home” to New York, where the despair dissipated. I’m quite fond of that station, and I’m eager to see what comes of its ongoing renovation.

[Many of the images below are actually slide shows; you can scroll left to see more ]

 

There’s much else about this city I’ve deeply appreciated — even loved. Even through it didn’t love me back. Even through I worked so much, and though that work made me so depressed, that I didn’t have nearly enough time to explore and embed as I would’ve liked.

So, to reclaim my experience from the campus calamities, and to clear the air as I make my way out of town, I want to celebrate those Philadelphia features that sustained me and charmed me, that embodied the city’s distinction as a gritty, vibrant, hard, endearing place.

First, the Free Library. It, like all libraries, deserves a much bigger budget to maintain its facilities and do all the amazing things, and if I were to stay I would’ve aspired to develop much closer relationships with — and to do my best to support — the whole institution. But during my short time there, the folks in the newspaper and arts divisions, in particular, were fantastic colleagues. Both departments hosted my classes and supported the production of our Philadelphia Local Media Field Guide. The Art Department hosts marvelously creative programs, and their Instagram feed, where they feature new titles, is a delight. The Newspaper folks invited me to take part in a great panel discussion about local archival legend Marion Stokes. The library’s west hallway also features a row of cubbies that invite the most clever diorama-style installations.

More book-related riches: Making Worlds Books, a progressive co-op; Iffy Books, a brilliant solarpunk/hacker bookshop that hosted my class to talk about communist media and community networks (I think we blew their future-consultant minds!); Ulises (oh, my heart!); Partner & Sons, which I liken to a very carefully edited Printed Matter-meets-Drawn & Quarterly; 50 Watts; Wooden Shoe, and others I’m certainly forgetting.

Speaking of media: I so deeply appreciate the city’s the vibrant local media scene: from PhillyCAM and Philly Community Wireless (both of whom contributed to my Local Media class) to WKDU (Drexel student radio!) and the Daily Pennsylvanian, Penn’s independent student newspaper, which does an admirable job of taking the institution to task and consistently reminding readers that Trump is a product of the business school

Philly’s also got the Inquirer, the largest urban newspaper run by a nonprofit — and that public commitment shows in its coverage. The paper employs some local legends, including national opinion columnist Will Bunch and local architecture + urbanism critic Inga Saffron. I especially appreciate Saffron’s focus on inter-city bus infrastructure — a vital but under-acknowledged and under-designed infrastructure serving working class travelers — and other humble-but-essential urban amenities. The Lenfest Institute, the Inquirer’s “non-profit, noncontrolling owner,” supports lots of local journalism efforts; they, too, contributed to my Local Media class. The People’s Media Fund and Resolve Philly are among myriad other local media advocates. As a Pennsylvania native and daughter to two Pennsylvania parents, I’m also grateful for Spotlight PA, which offers investigative and public-service journalism across the state — particularly in red, rural areas with no local news sources, or with zombie papers run by hedge funds and AI.

Speaking of public service: the Fairmount Water Works is a fantastic example of public pedagogy promoting infrastructural literacy. It reminds us of what a marvel it is that we have access to clean, potable water. The Water Works also hosted a fabulous exhibition on the history of segregation in public pools.

Speaking of public infrastructure: TinyWPA is awesome, too. They’re a citizen-led design-build organization that works with lots of city agencies. Relatedly, a good neighborhood hardware store is essential, and Rittenhouse Hardware — a social infrastructure animated by their dog, Carl, the goodest of good boys — is the platonic corner shop. And I’ll never forget Doggie Style, a local chain of pet shops that just happened to have an outpost a block from our house. We took our dog Inge in on occasion for a bath and a nail trim — but I was there almost every day I was in town to walk the dogs that were up for adoption.  Some of the bigger pit bulls were difficult to place — given breed prejudice and landlord restrictions — and it broke my heart to watch them grow more and more withdrawn and despondent as they wiled away their weeks in their little rooms. Yet ultimately I saw nearly all of my buddies welcomed into new, loving homes — and the few that had a more difficult time finding their families were transferred to suburban shops where homeowners with bigger yards might be better able to accommodate their needs. Below is a selection of my pals, including, at the top of the deck, Phoebe, a four-month old gal found as a weeks’-old stray, whom I’d hoped to see off to her forever home before we left, but alas. I hope her family finds her soon.

I also loved the little turtles that sunned themselves on branches in the Schuylkill River, whose dog park was another highlight. I appreciated that the bridge to the trail offered a balcony view of the dogs at play.

Speaking of friends: we met lots of spectacular people in Philly. I was so out-of-the-loop on campus, and so many of the folks who were central to my recruitment left either right before or shortly after I arrived, that I didn’t make many strong connections there, but I did find a few confidants: the Karens (both phenomenal), the Ians, Litty, Emily, Rahul, Amber, Catherine, Jess, Keith, Jared, and others. Our neighbors at home were amazing. Edwin, Brian, Marina, Adrienne, Erkan, Jürgen, Susan, Tom, Lisa, Dan, Ian…. And through the renovations in our 200-year-old house — which we planned to stay in for 20 years, as I retired into this so-great-on-paper job, and which ultimately erased any financial gains said job may have provided — we met a brigade of skilled, kind, and fun contractors: Josh and Gregg, Paul and Frank, Tommy, Tim and Karl, Fred, Glenn, Matt and his team. I love my Swarthmore friends — Patty, Tim, Andy, Amanda, et al — too.

And speaking of craftspeople: there’s lots of good lettering around the city — like this Copperplate on the Municipal Services Building and the Parks & Rec signs, as well as the sans serif signage on Pierce College and the Department of Public Health building, both near our house.

And of course so many fantastic murals. My favorite is probably this Amy Sherald on 11th and Sansom, but I also love the David Guinn piece we pass by every day on our walks with Inge. I’ll always remember Emilio Poppe’s stirring Civic Views installation, curated by Mural Arts’ Jameson Paige at City Hall (and later featured in the Whitney Biennial!). The show, initiated years ago, was movingly prescient in its commitment to honoring civic workers during the early months of the Trump regime. Emilio and Jameson invited me to join State Senator Nikil Saval to speak amidst the installation about civic space — and that event, which came near the end of my time in Philly, was a welcome opportunity for connection after two years of perplexing and disheartening alienation in this town.

 

Another Philly arts staple was, of course, the University of the Arts — and we were so disappointed to witness its dishonorable collapse from a few blocks away. I long admired its legendary book arts program, and I have a friend who was recruited to develop an exciting new curatorial program, only to have the whole thing evaporate a year after his arrival. Several local universities — except, of course, for the gigantic, wealthy one — offered to step up to salvage the school. As tragic as the whole debacle was — for both Philadelphia and arts education in general — I was heartened to learn that Scout, a local woman-led firm, has been charged with redeveloping parts of the campus into an arts-centric complex, with studios, artist housing, exhibition space, and more.

I was also so impressed with Scout’s recognition that the University’s abrupt closure incited a great deal of trauma — so, as a first step in their adaptive reuse process, they hosted a “celebration of life” to mourn and commemorate the university’s legacy. I attended some of the events and was deeply moved. I’m eager to continue watching this project emerge from afar.

Scout also developed the Bok Building, an old school-turned-workspace for artists, makers, and nonprofits. The ground floor bakery, Machine Shop, is fantastic.

More good bread: Ursa and Manna. Croissants: J’aime! They opened a second, small outpost a block away from our house shortly after we arrived, and they — particularly the effervescent baristas, many of whom were University of the Arts musical theater grads — became a part of our daily routine. Shortly before we departed, the owner suffered serious injuries in a bike accident, and they closed up the nearby shop — which offered a sad, symbolically fitting closure to our time in the neighborhood. We’re wishing them all well.

More food: the summer salads at High Street are super. Kalaya‘s among the best Thai we’ve ever had. Honeysuckle is amazing; we did one of the bodega dinners at the old West Philly shop and attended the soft launch of their new, grand space on North Broad. I also really love the mint iced tea at Cosmic Cafe, a spot at the end of Boathouse Row, along the Schuylkill River Trail, that employs people with disabilities, features really earnest local singer-songwriters in the patio outside, and draws a daily roller-skate-dance brigade

And speaking of performance: I wish had seen more music, theater, and fine art. I escaped to NYC so frequently I failed to seek out more of Philly’s riches, and I regret that. Still, I came to know and appreciate the Fabric Workshop, the Institute for Contemporary Art, and the Museum for Wood Art, which will undoubtedly draw me down from NYC for continued visits. Nearby is one of my favorite aspirational clothing shops, Rennes. And just northwest of the city is another all-time-favorite museum of wood: the Wharton Esherick Museum. I covet his library stool. Northeast are two other greats: the George Nakashima House, Studio, and Workshop, and the Mercer Museum, a wunderkammer of historical tools in a castle.

While I regret not seeing much live music — again, work consumed nearly all of my evening hours, and I failed to cash in my tickets to see Still Plants at Solar Myth — I also did attend a few incredibly memorable performances: Courtney Barnett played the sanctuary at the First Unitarian Church. The School for Temporary Liveness, held at the Rotunda and Slought, was filled with thoughtfully curated performance and academic talks — like Kevin Quashie’s — that absolutely constituted performance art in their own right. Tyshawn Storey’s arresting “Be Holding” was staged on a basketball court at Girard College. And Julianknxx hosted “Chorus in Flight” on the Great Stair at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Both spectacular.

I was also delighted to discover that Philly has had a vibrant shoegaze scene (although they seem to interpret the term rather loosely!). One of my favorite albums of 2024 — Mannequin Pussy, who are certainly not shoegaze — emerged from Philly. Alex G started to grow on me, too.

Another favorite spot in the city — one I’ve visited repeatedly, starting well before we moved to Philly — is the Barnes Foundation. Regrettably, I never saw its original manifestation out in Merion, PA, and some of the purists argue that its new downtown version pales in comparison. But I think the Tod Williams and Billie Tsien space is gorgeous. The (post-)impressionist collection is fine, but I’m most taken by the juxtapositions: the paintings, the frames, the metalwork, the furnishings, the wall textures, the light, the courtyard plantings. All the glorious idiosyncrasy.

I also thoroughly enjoyed the small-but-mighty “history of school lunch” exhibition I saw at the Science History Institute, and Pepón Osorio’s stirring “Convalescence” installation in the lobby of Jefferson University’s health sciences campus; I happened upon the latter on my way back from a mammogram. The show was so unexpectedly poignant I recommended it to the students in my Methods class, so we took a field trip.

Other favorite spaces: all the Frank Furness buildings, Athena Tacha’s Connections at Matthias Baldwin Park (ground-level photos don’t do it justice!), the Rail Park (lots of promise!), and the block-long labor-of-love garden behind the parking garage on Kater Street.

I’ll close with one of our final stops. Calder Gardens opened just a few weeks before our move. It’s near both the Barnes Foundation and Matthias Baldwin Park. There’s so much about Herzog & de Meuron’s new building and Piet Oudolf’s landscape that seemed to encapsulate my experience in the city: the newly-planted, scrubby gardens just waiting to grow into wild, untamed fields; the subterranean space, filled with light, bursting with color and whimsy. Effervescence in stillness.

Alexander Rower, president of the Calder Foundation, said of his grandfather’s work: “The poetry happens between the objects—the negative space is where the art happens.” The last three years have felt like a void for me: I lost my energy, my health, my confidence. I lost interest in my work and the capacity to have ideas. My dad lost his beloved woodshop — plus all his tools, and 40,000 board feet of cherry, walnut, tiger and bird’s-eye maple, mahogany, purple heart, and some really stellar pieces of walnut crotch — to a fire. For a decade now, we’ve been incrementally losing mom to Alzheimer’s. Our family has lost many friends to cancer. I’ve lost my trajectory. I left my home, my webs of connection, and failed to find new ones here. I’ve strayed from the career that brought me to this place.

After a couple years of failed attempts to force myself to produce, to maintain the pace I had set 25 years ago, I decided instead to dedicate the final couple months of my time in Philadelphia to nourishment: to filling that internal void with the creative work and wonder of others. My negative space, my own internal clearing, made space for their art to “happen” in me. In Calder’s new Philadelphia installation, Adam Gopnik wrote in the New Yorker, “a mobile begins to stir as you pass, elegantly or uneasily, shifting with the faintest disturbance. Speak softly and it moves.” Calder spoke to me. All those tiny, accumulated stirrings and whispers of the past few years — those gestures that felt futile, and even at times regressive; the fallowness that seemed to portend my own dissolution and irrelevance  — they’ve moved me. And I’m ready to move on.
